chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Harun ibn Muslim, from Ibn Sa'dan, from Mas'adah ibn Sadah, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon him), who said:

Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no bequest for an heir, and no acknowledgment of debt.' He means: if the sick person acknowledges a debt to one of the heirs, it is not valid for him. The way to understand this report is to carry it on taqiyyah (dissimulation), because it includes 'no bequest for an heir and no acknowledgment of debt.' And we have explained that his acknowledgment to the heirs is valid. And we will explain later that he may bequeath to those other than the heirs if there is something that needs mentioning, although we have fully covered this in our Great Book, so whoever wishes to stop at it, let him stop there. And it is possible that what is meant by the report is that there is no acknowledgment of the debt in what exceeds one-third if it is suspect, because we have explained that this is not permissible if the one acknowledging is not trustworthy and acceptable, and that it remains valid in the one-third and below.
ai.seo_question: Does a sick person's acknowledgment of debt to an heir count as a bequest or a valid debt?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves the tension between the prohibition of bequeathing to heirs and the validity of debt acknowledgment by interpreting the hadith through taqiyyah or limiting the suspect portion to the one-third share. This reflects the Shia juristic principle that a dying person’s admission of debt to an heir is valid but subject to scrutiny regarding the 'one-third' rule applicable to bequests. The commentary draws from al-Tusi’s broader legal corpus to clarify that such acknowledgments are permissible provided they do not exceed the discretionary share unless the heir is deemed trustworthy.
